newsitem.title: UK: Medical editors form anti-fraud committee.
newsitem.headline: Medical editors form anti-fraud committee.

text.p: British medical editors joined forces on Friday to fight what they fear is a growing problem of research fraud.
They said the committee would examine possible fraud cases, publish a report and consider teaching on ways to avoid fraud.

"We need effective systems for preventing, detecting and investigating research misconduct and for imposing punishment, and it will obviously be sensible to put the emphasis on preventing," British Medical Journal editor Richard Smith said in an editorial.
"We still do not know how many cases of research misconduct there are in Britain, but it is becoming increasingly difficult to argue that cases are isolated and rare."

Smith wrote: "The United States has many cases because it has more effective methods for identifying them. In Britain we seem to be leaving it to pharmaceutical companies, a private agency and the media to discover most cases." This was "shameful," he added.

The new Committee on Publication Ethics would include the editors of Gut, the BMJ, the Lancet, the British Journal of Anaesthesia, the Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery, the British Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology and other journals.
Such publications are influential because they not only publish new research papers but also give them a standing because they subject the reports to review by other experts in the field.
The issue of fraud was highlighted in Britain with the 1995 case of Malcolm Pearce, who was found to have forged a series of papers.
An Edinburgh physician was struck off the list of registered physicians last week for falsifying data in a clinical trial.
